explanations.explanation: Right at the top, the psalm says, "Praise the LORD from the heavens; praise Him in the highest places." (Psalm 148:1) The psalm writer starts way up high and works his way down. I think that's a smart way to run a list, because nobody has to wonder where to start.

Jerusalem is a good guess, friend, but it's not in this psalm at all. The very first call goes out "from the heavens," and then "in the highest places." (Psalm 148:1) This list starts way above any city.

The temple makes sense, since that's where a lot of praise happened. But the psalm doesn't start there. It says, "Praise the LORD from the heavens; praise Him in the highest places." (Psalm 148:1) The writer is looking way up before he looks anywhere near a building.

Yes, angels, friend. The psalm says, "Praise Him, all His angels; praise Him, all His heavenly hosts." (Psalm 148:2) They go first in the heavens. I once had an angel show up at my drawer, and I'm telling you, that's a choir member you want.

Prophets did speak for God, but they aren't in this verse. Up in the heavens, the psalm says, "Praise Him, all His angels; praise Him, all His heavenly hosts." (Psalm 148:2) The angels are the first ones called on.

Priests served in the temple, so I see why you picked them. But this part of the psalm is still up in the heavens, and it says, "Praise Him, all His angels; praise Him, all His heavenly hosts." (Psalm 148:2) Angels get the first call, not priests.

Not quite, friend. The psalm writer keeps climbing after the sun, moon and stars. The very next verse says, "Praise Him, O highest heavens, and you waters above the skies." (Psalm 148:4) So there's more sky left, and it all gets called on.

That's right. The writer isn't done with the sky yet. He says, "Praise Him, O highest heavens, and you waters above the skies." (Psalm 148:4) Even after all those shining stars, he keeps looking higher.

explanations.answer: He commanded and they were created
explanations.explanation: That's the reason, friend. The psalm says, "Let them praise the name of the LORD, for He gave the command and they were created." (Psalm 148:5) He spoke, and they were made. That's the whole reason given.

explanations.answer: They were made to serve people
explanations.explanation: That sounds reasonable, but this psalm doesn't say it. The reason it gives is, "for He gave the command and they were created." (Psalm 148:5) The praise is tied to who made them, not to who they serve.

explanations.answer: They live closest to His throne
explanations.explanation: Nice guess, but no throne shows up in this part of the psalm. The reason is, "for He gave the command and they were created." (Psalm 148:5) It's about Him creating them, not about where they live.

Yep, that's what it says. "He established them forever and ever; He issued a decree that will never pass away." (Psalm 148:6) Forever and ever, and the decree never passes away. I can't even keep a batch of cookies around past Tuesday.
This one is true, friend. The psalm says, "He established them forever and ever; He issued a decree that will never pass away." (Psalm 148:6) The decree stays. It never passes away.

Yes, the earth. The psalm says, "Praise the LORD from the earth, all great sea creatures and ocean depths." (Psalm 148:7) After all that sky, the writer brings the call down to ground level. Well, ocean level, but you get it.

The sanctuary is a holy place, but it isn't the next stop on this list. The psalm says, "Praise the LORD from the earth, all great sea creatures and ocean depths." (Psalm 148:7) After the heavens, the call goes to the earth.

Zion is a name Scripture uses a lot, but it isn't in this part of the psalm. The next call is, "Praise the LORD from the earth, all great sea creatures and ocean depths." (Psalm 148:7) From the heavens, he comes down to the whole earth.
That's it. The psalm calls it "powerful wind fulfilling His word." (Psalm 148:8) The wind is doing what He said. I wish my oven timer listened that well.
Rain would fit with weather, friend, but the psalm doesn't say that. It says "powerful wind fulfilling His word." (Psalm 148:8) The wind's job here is fulfilling His word.
That's a big job for the wind, but it isn't in this verse. The psalm says "powerful wind fulfilling His word." (Psalm 148:8) Nothing here about nations, just the wind doing what He said.
True, friend. The psalm says, "fruit trees and all cedars." (Psalm 148:9) The trees get a spot on the list, right along with the mountains and the hills.
It's actually true. The psalm calls on "mountains and all hills, fruit trees and all cedars." (Psalm 148:9) So the trees are in the choir, from the fruit trees to the big cedars.

explanations.answer: Kings and rulers of the earth
explanations.explanation: Right, the kings and rulers. The psalm says, "kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and all rulers of the earth." (Psalm 148:11) They lead off the people part of the list. I think they might have been surprised to be in the same line as the sea creatures.

Priests and Levites served in the temple, so that's a fair guess. But the psalm doesn't name them here. When it gets to people, it says, "kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and all rulers of the earth." (Psalm 148:11) Rulers come first.
Good guess, but they aren't on this list. The psalm says, "kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and all rulers of the earth." (Psalm 148:11) The kings and rulers are at the top for people.
Not quite, friend. The psalm says, "young men and maidens, old and young together." (Psalm 148:12) The word is together. They're called on as one group.
Right. The writer doesn't split them up. He says, "young men and maidens, old and young together." (Psalm 148:12) Old and young are called on together.
That's the reason. The psalm says, "Let them praise the name of the LORD, for His name alone is exalted." (Psalm 148:13) Nobody else is lifted up like that. His name alone.

explanations.answer: His throne rests on the earth
explanations.explanation: The psalm doesn't say that, friend. The reason given is, "for His name alone is exalted; His splendor is above the earth and the heavens." (Psalm 148:13) His splendor is above the earth, not resting on it.

explanations.answer: His mercy fills the whole earth
explanations.explanation: Mercy is a lovely thing to praise Him for, and other psalms talk about it. But this one gives a different reason: "for His name alone is exalted." (Psalm 148:13) That's what the writer points to here.

Yes, that's the last description. The psalm ends with "of Israel, a people near to Him." (Psalm 148:14) After all that sky and sea, the writer ends on a people who are near. I'd say that's a warm way to finish.

explanations.answer: A people sent to the nations
explanations.explanation: Sent to the nations isn't what this psalm says. The last verse says, "of Israel, a people near to Him." (Psalm 148:14) The word it uses is near.
Waiting is a good word for plenty of Bible moments, friend, but not this one. The psalm says, "of Israel, a people near to Him." (Psalm 148:14) Near, not waiting.
